CHINESE MODE OF PRropaGatTinGc Fruit ‘Traees.—The ingenious people of China
have a common method of propagating several kinds of fruit trees, which of late
years has been practised with success in Bengal The method is simply this :—
They strip a ring of bark, about an inch in width, from oa bearing branch, ¢ur-
round the place with a ball of fat earth, or Joam, bound fast to the branch with a
piece of matting: over this they suspend a pot or horn, with water, having a small
hoie in the bottom just suthcient to let the water drop, in order to keep the earth
constantly moist. The branch throws new roots into the earth jast above the
place where the ring of bark was stripped off The operation is performed in the
spring, and the branch is sawed offand put into the ground at the fall of the leaf,
The following year it will bear fruit.

To Prevent BiossoM AND FPRUIT-TREES FROM BEING DAMAGED BY EARLY Sprinao

branches of a fruit-t.ee in blossom, and the end of it brought down, so as to terini-
nate ina bucket of water; and should a slight frost take place in the night time,
in that ewse the tree will not be affeeted by the frost; but a film of ice of consider-
able thickness, Will be formed on the surface of the bucket in which the rope's

muller, in the same manner as painters grind their white-lead, &e.; but where
these conveniences are not at hand, the ingredients may be mixed ina large pan,
and well beat up with a wooden spatula, Two coats of this composition being ne-
cessary, the first may be rather thin; but the second should be as thick as it can
eonveniently be worked. This most excellent composition for preserving the
wood, is highly preferable to the customary method of laying on tar and ochre,

How to cer Fret Trees To your Lixino.—In October or November take a |
branch ofan appl or pear tree, such as suits your taste. Take off down to the

and shut the pores of the wood thoroughly; ther bury in the ground all but the
last year’s growth. If placed in good ground, and well taken care of, you will
have fruit in five or six years. I have sometimes dipped the Jower end in melted
resin, but yet think burning preferable. L have a tree near my door that is nine
fect high, and well propo: tioned, that I took trom a graft four years ago; to this
resin was applied; and whatever sprouts sprang up next summer were bent down
and becanie roots. We can get fruit considerably quicker in this way than from
reed; and we know what we have growing, and when grown the whole tree is of |
the same kind; and whatever sprouts come from the roots in after years can be |
transplanted without grafting. In cases of drought the first year they should be
watered,

Comrorts FOR CATTILE.—Good stables, good food, and good water, are the prime
comforts fur cattle in winter. For summer, whatever else they may have, how
can they get on without a seratching pole?) Rev. Sydney Smith, of England, was
something of a farmer, and used to visit his cattle daily; and feed and pat them»
until they knew his voice and welcomed his coming. He used to do all in his
power to make them comfortable. He has been heard to say, “I am for all cheap
luxuries, even for animals; now animals have a passion for scratching their back
bones; they break down your gates and palings to effect this. Look! this is my
universal seratcher, a sharp-edged pole, resting on a high and low post, adapted to
every height, from a horse toa lamb. Even the Edinburgh reviewer can take his
turn; you have no idea how popular itis. I have not had a gate broken down |
since I putitup. I have itin all my flelds.” |
